subject: How to use imposeMissing from simsem?

messages.author: e3cd7ac95409208e
messages.subject: How to use imposeMissing from simsem?
parts:
Hello. I'm somewhat new to missing data and I'm trying to learn its effects (and remedies) through simulation. But it seems like I'm getting stuck in how to impose a missing data pattern in my simulation that matches the assumption of Missing At Random (MAR). This is the code I'm running. I'm running it within the context of multiple regression, which I am much more familiar with:

library(MASS)
library(simsem)


## correlation among predictors and the covariate for the missing data
r1 <- 0.3
r2 <- 0.5


#sample size, population regression coefficients and residual variance
n <- 100
b0 <- 1
b1 <- 0.0
b2 <- 0.3
sigm <- 1


#1000 repetitions and vectors to store results
reps <- 1000
B1 <- double(reps)
B2 <- double(reps)
pv1 <- double(reps)
pv2 <- double(reps)


for(i in 1:reps){

##this part generates the complete dataset from a multivariate normal distribution
S <- matrix(c(1 ,r1, r2, 0, r1,  1, r2, 0, r2, r2, 1, r2, 0,  0, r2, 1),4,4)
a <- mvrnorm(n, c(0,0,0,0), S)
e <- rnorm(n, 0, sigm)

x <- a[,1]
z <- a[,2]
c <- a[,3]
y <- a[,4]


#here i create the regression model
y <- b0 + b1*x + b2*z + e


#here i impose the missing data pattern
datam <- data.frame(y,x,z,c)
mdat <- imposeMissing(datam, cov=c("c"), pmMAR = 0.4)


##here i estimate my regression models over and over again
colnames(mdat) <- c("Y","X","Z","C")

## extract coefficients
B1[i]<-coef(lm(Y ~ X + Z,  data=mdat))[2]
B2[i]<-coef(lm(Y ~ X + Z,  data=mdat))[3]

## p.value for the t-test of the regression coefficients
pv1[i]<-summary(lm(Y ~ X + Z,  data=mdat))$coefficients[2,4]
pv2[i]<-summary(lm(Y ~ X + Z,  data=mdat))$coefficients[3,4]
}


I thought that I would find bias in my parameter estimates and inflated type 1 error rates since the lm() function handles missing data using listwise deletion. However, when I calculate the mean of my parameter estimates and the empirical rejection rates, this is what I find:

> mean(B1)
[1] -0.005532745

> mean(B2)
[1] 0.3089108
 
> sum(pv1<.05)/reps
[1] 0.056

> sum(pv2<.05)/reps
[1] 0.48

Even though I'm asking imposeMissing() for 40% missing data following a MAR pattern the results of my simulation indicate that there is very little (if any) bias of the regression coefficients and that the coefficients both maintain Type 1 error rate and adequate power (for that sample size and effect size).

I'm not sure what I'm doing wrong. There's clearly something I'm not grasping in how to generate MAR data. 

The weird thing is that if I do this simulation in the much simpler case of a bivariate correlation I DO obtain the results I would expect (bias, inflated type 1 error rate, reduced power, etc.). So I guess I'm missing something here as far as the process in which I'm generating data.

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: How to use imposeMissing from simsem?
parts:
Might have something to do with the fact that Z is highly correlated with the covariate that explains missingness.  And you are imposing missingness on all variables (Y, X, Z) using the same mechanism, so most of the time one variable is missing, the whole row is missing.  So among the complete rows, the same regression model still holds, and the only thing that should change is your power (I think).  But you are right -- the effects of missing mechanisms are more complicated than just MCAR / MAR.  Sophia Rabe-Hasketh showed some odd situations in a 2014 presentation you can access here:

http://www.modeling.uconn.edu/m3c/assets/File/Rabe-Hesketh.pdf

You might find some clues in there, or at least references for further reading.  But doing simulations like you are doing might be the fastest way to learn about any particular scenario you are worried about in a real-data situation.

By the way, you seem to redundantly generate Y from the regression model as well as using mvrnorm(), where in S it is uncorrelated with anything else.  Perhaps you mean to generate the uncorrelated errors "e" as the 4th row/column in S, instead of generating e independently in a call to univariate rnorm().  Including e in S (and then constructing Y in your regression model) would enable you to see the effect of having the covariate correlate with the errors, which I assume  would introduce bias in point estimates and Type I error rates.

Also, you might find the last example on the ?impose help page useful.  It demonstrates how to use a logistic regression formula to apply MAR, where the intercept is the overall proportion missing you want, and the slopes indicate the effect of the covariate (on whichever particular variable(s) you want to have missingness).  

Terry

messages.author: e3cd7ac95409208e
messages.subject: Re: How to use imposeMissing from simsem?
parts:
Hello Terry. Thank you for taking the time to look at my code, your answer was very helpful. You see, the reason of why I chose high correlations between the covariate and the predictors was based on this other (simpler) simulation that I did when I found that unless the covariate was correlated with the predictors of interest, the missing data mechanism had virtually no effect in terms of bias/type 1 error rates.

For instance, if you run this code:

library(MASS)
library(simsem)

### correlation between x & y
r1 <- 0.0

### correlation between the covariate and x and y
covr <- 0.0

## sample size
n <- 100

B1 <- double(reps)
pv1 <- double(reps)
reps <- 1000

for (i in 1:reps){
a <- mvrnorm(n,c(0,0,0),matrix(c(1,r1,covr,r1,1, covr,covr,covr,1),3,3))

x <- a[,1]
y <- a[,2]
c <- a[,3]

datam <- data.frame(y,x,c)
mdat <- imposeMissing(datam, cov=c("c"), pmMAR = 0.4)

B1[i]<-cor(mdat, use="complete.obs")[1,2]
pv1[i]<-cor.test(mdat$x,mdat$y, use="complete.obs")$p.value
}

The results you obtain are basically that the missing data mechanism has no effect:

> mean(B1)
[1] -0.001792044
> sum(pv1<.05)/reps
[1] 0.052

But if you change this:

r1 <- 0.0
covr <- 0.5 ### THE CORRELATION BETWEEN THE COVARIATE AND X,Y IS NOT 0
n <- 100
B1 <- double(reps)
pv1 <- double(reps)
reps <- 1000

and re-run the code what you find is:

> mean(B1)
[1] -0.1486644
> sum(pv1<.05)/reps
[1] 0.203

So now I have both a negative bias AND an inflated Type 1 error rate, which is what I would expect from a MAR mechanism since by specifying 

cor(mdat, use="complete.obs")

I'm basically doing listwise deletion, which should fail as a missing data technique when in presence of MAR. So, at least in this simpler case, what the theory dictates and what my code is doing overlaps which is good. 

From this simulation experiment, it seems like the covariate that generates the missingness must be highly correlated with the variables of interest for the missing data mechanism to have an effect on parameter estimates/inference. In general (from this smaller simulation) the higher the correlation between the covariate 'c' and the variables 'x' and 'y', the worse (where worse means more bias and higher type 1 error rates) the effect of the missing data mechanism will be.

I tried to apply that same principle to the regression simulation to find an effect, but as you can see I failed. The reason of why I "redundantly" generated Y was to try and keep this same principle (i.e. covariate must be highly correlated with both the predictors and the dependent variable for it to have an effect) but until you pointed this out I realized that by specifying y <- model + error I break the correlation between Y and C.  

Your observation, however, that when one piece of data is missing the whole row is probably missing is true. I guess then I need a different way to generate missingness using more than one covariate? I find it a little bit strange that so much work needs to be put in order to mimic something like a MAR mechanism on  a multiple regression with just 2 predictors. But there's something definitely wrong in the way I'm approaching this for the regression case.

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: How to use imposeMissing from simsem?
parts:
I don't know that there's anything "wrong" with what you're doing.  We never know the real mechanism (unless it is planned missingness), just like we never know the true parameters we are trying to estimate.  So the simulations are just a way for you to see what would happen in some plausible scenarios that you can imagine and model.

Terry
